children: By Hannah Pedone
One fund manager says the continued uncertainty makes Nvidia 'vulnerable' to more selling, even as the stock has erased over $900 billion in market value in the past seven trading sessions
Nvidia's stock has been sinking amid corporate tumult in recent weeks.
Nvidia's stock was on track to book a decline for the seventh week in a row - a stretch of consecutive losses not seen in nearly two decades.

A cascade of factors has left the stock reeling - most notably former CEO Jensen Huang's resignation and the Nvidia board's investigation into whether he compromised national security or revealed corporate secrets. But the stock had been under pressure even before that, with investors questioning the sustainability of artificial-intelligence demand.
Nvidia shares (NVDA) haven't fallen for seven weeks in a row since July 2008, when the company issued a profit warning and was working to address defects in some of its chips.
Shares of Nvidia were trading 12% lower on Friday. They've lost nearly 17% so far this week and are more than 43% lower than their peak close achieved in early October.

Nvidia's stock has fallen for seven trading sessions in a row, over which it has shed roughly $907 billion in market capitalization. That's more than the market value of JPMorgan Chase (JPM), which has an $835 billion market cap, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

By market value, Nvidia is now the fourth-largest U.S. company, falling below Google parent Alphabet (GOOGL) (GOOG) for the first time since April 2024, according to Dow Jones Market Data. Nvidia's market cap is now $3.28 trillion, while Alphabet's is at $3.32 trillion.
The stock's "weakness despite strong earnings shows how much it will take to restore confidence." David Miller, CIO at Catalyst Funds, told MarketWatch.
On Tuesday, Nvidia reported blockbuster earnings results and raised its revenue outlook for next year, but that wasn't enough to stem the bleeding.
Seaport Research analyst Jay Goldberg told MarketWatch that fund managers who previously held Nvidia because it was a "safety stock" are now "rotating out" amid the turmoil.
So what comes next?
Goldberg expects things to stabilize next week. "I don't think it keeps falling," he said - though adding that "there is no one in a hurry to buy it until we know who the next CEO is."
But Miller said Nvidia's stock is "vulnerable" to more selling. The length of the losing streak alone "tells us very little about where the bottom is," he told MarketWatch.

"A sharp rebound is certainly possible, but I would want greater clarity on permanent leadership and the investigations, along with continued execution on customer demand and product deliveries, before becoming confident in a sustained recovery," he said.
In a Friday news conference, President Donald Trump said he would "like to see Jensen make a big apology and go back" to Nvidia.
"We have to protect our brilliant people. Jensen is one of them," he added.
-Hannah Pedone
